migrationNotes: Spine: kitchen scales with a bag of marbles hidden in one pan. Whatever you take from one pan you take from the other, and that single rule, written as an equation and paired with the opposite move for each operation, gets the hidden number on its own.
Opener asks nothing: intro.hook.questionId is removed. The marbles puzzle (…-hook, key 8) is the first practice screen, after the teaching screen that uses 6 loose marbles and 10.
Order changed on purpose: one-move solving (…-3, 4x = 20) now comes before the two-move examples. The worked example gains a second self-explanation (…-check-inverse).
…-check-both-sides (numeric, key 7) is left out of the steps; its question is unchanged in the draft. It would repeat what …-hook and …-1 already ask.
Figures: equation_balance on every screen that has an equation; the balance cannot yet apply a move to both pans (see figure-wishlist.md).

lesson.title: Keeping the balance

lead.text: Start with scales that are level. Say the left pan holds a bag of marbles and 6 loose ones, and the right pan holds 10 marbles. Lift the 6 loose marbles out of the left pan and that pan rises, so the scales tip. Take 6 marbles out of the right pan as well and they settle level again.
Now the left pan holds only the bag, and the right pan holds the 4 marbles left over from the 10. The scales are level, so the bag weighs the same as 4 marbles. You never opened it.

The method comes down to one rule. If two amounts are equal and you take the same amount from each, what is left is still equal. The same goes for adding the same amount to each pan, or for doubling or halving both. A change to one pan alone breaks the balance, and then what you work out about the bag is wrong.
Scales are a picture of something you already know. An equation is a pair of sides that are equal, and the next screen puts the scales and the equation side by side.

diagram.alt: A pair of kitchen scales. A tied bag and 6 loose marbles in the left pan balance 10 marbles in the right pan. Three views show taking 6 marbles from the left pan only, which tips the beam, and from both pans, which levels it again.
diagram.caption: Take marbles from one pan only and the scales tip. Take the same number from both and they stay level. Use the buttons to move through the three views.

lead.text: Every marble weighs the same, and the scales are level. Work it out the way the scales would.

reveal.text: You took the 3 spare marbles off both pans. The next screen writes that move down.

lead.text: Now write the scales down. Call the number of marbles in the bag x. In your puzzle the left pan holds x and 3 loose marbles, and the right pan holds 11, so level scales say:

The two pans are the two sides of the equation, and the equals sign says they weigh the same. Take 3 from both sides and the left side becomes x on its own, while the right side becomes 11 − 3. That is the move you made with the marbles, and it gives x = 8.

afterFigure.text: Now see what a one-sided move does. Take 3 from the left side alone and you get x = 11. Put 11 back into the original equation and the left side comes to 14, while the right side is still 11. The balance is out, because the move changed the puzzle.
So the rule is to do the same thing to both sides. When you do, the new equation has exactly the same solution as the old one, and you can use it to simplify. The next question tests that.

lead.text: The balance shows 2x + 6 on the left and 18 on the right. You want a simpler equation with exactly the same solution.

reveal.text: Whichever move you picked, ask whether it acted on both sides. Subtracting 6 from each turns 2x + 6 = 18 into 2x = 12, with the same solution and a simpler shape.

lead.text: The scales say what you may do. To use them you need a plan for getting x on its own, and the plan is to look at what has been done to x and undo it.

If 5 has been added to a number, taking 5 away puts the number back, so adding and subtracting are opposites. Multiplying and dividing are opposites in the same way: a number trebled and then divided by 3 is the number you began with.

An opposite move is called an inverse operation. On the scales it is something you can picture. Say three identical bags balance 12 marbles. Split each pan into three equal parts, which is dividing both sides by 3. One bag then balances 4 marbles.

afterFigure.text: To get x alone, find what has been done to it and apply the inverse operation to both sides. One move is never allowed. You cannot divide by 0, because nothing undoes multiplying by 0: every number multiplied by 0 gives 0, so there is no way back to the number you started with.
The next question needs just one move.

lead.text: Four bags in one pan balance 20 marbles in the other. Decide which inverse operation gets x alone, and apply it to both sides.

reveal.text: One move was enough. The inverse of × 4 is ÷ 4, and applying it to both sides left x alone.

lead.text: Most equations ask for more than one move. Suppose four identical bags and 3 loose marbles sit in the left pan, and 19 marbles sit in the right. Written down, that is:

You can't split the left pan into four equal parts while the loose marbles are mixed in with the bags. So the loose marbles come off first, and the same number has to come off the right pan. Subtracting 3 from both sides leaves four bags balancing 16 marbles:

afterFigure.text: Now the pan can be split. Divide both sides by 4 and one bag balances 4 marbles, so x = 4. The check is the one from the first lesson: put 4 into the original equation, and the left side is 4 × 4 + 3 = 19, which matches the right side.
The next example writes the same two moves as equations, naming the opposite move at each line.

lead.text: Here the moves are written as equations. Each line names a move and shows the result, and each move is applied to both sides.

workedSteps.text: Subtract 2 from both sides. It undoes the + 2.
Now the × 3 has to go. Which move undoes it?

lead.text: Your turn for the last two lines.

workedSteps.text: Divide both sides by 2. Which x makes 2x = 12 true?

steps.headline: When the numbers go below zero

lead.text: So far every number in the equations has been positive. Equations can have minus signs and negative numbers too, and the same two ideas apply. Take 2x − 4 = −10. The 4 has been taken away from 2x, and the opposite of taking away is adding, so add 4 to both sides.

The left side becomes 2x. The right side becomes −10 + 4. To work that out, think of a temperature of 10 degrees below zero that rises by 4 degrees. It is now 6 below zero, so −10 + 4 = −6. The equation reads 2x = −6.

afterFigure.text: Dividing finishes the job. Share −6 between two and each share is −3, because a negative number divided by a positive number is negative. So x = −3. Check by putting −3 into the original: 2 × (−3) is −6, and −6 − 4 is −10, which matches the right side.
A negative answer is allowed. Nothing in the method asks for x to be positive. The last question has a minus sign and a negative right side, and the same moves solve it.

lead.text: Here 9 is taken away from 3x and the right side is negative. Decide which move undoes the minus, then check your answer in the original equation.

lesson.orientation: Justify each step of a rearrangement by naming the operation applied to both sides.
lesson.nextAction: Unwind an expression by reversing the order its operations were applied in.

blocks.text: Picture a pair of old kitchen scales, with a pan on each side. In the left pan sits a bag of marbles, tied shut, with a few loose marbles beside it. The right pan holds a heap of marbles. The scales sit exactly level, and every marble weighs the same.

The puzzle is how many marbles the bag holds, and you aren't allowed to open it. In the last lesson you tried numbers until one fitted, which is fine for a small puzzle. The scales offer a way that needs no guessing, and it starts from a question about what you can do to them while they stay level.
This lesson follows that question. It turns the scales into an equation and finds the one rule that keeps them level. The rule then gets a hidden number on its own.

intro.promise: By the end you'll know why doing the same to both sides keeps an equation true, and use it to solve for x.

recap.keyIdea: An equation stays true when you do the same thing to both sides, so you can undo the operations on x with their inverses until x stands alone.

blocks.text: You found the bag on the scales, then did the same with letters: 3x + 2 = 23 became 3x = 21 and then x = 7. A minus sign worked the same way, and you reached x = −2 in 3x − 9 = −15 by adding 9 to both sides first.

recap.nextHook: In every example so far the moves came in an order the example gave you. Next you'll see why that order is the right one, and what to do when x has more layers around it, including a part in brackets.

questions.prompt: A bag of marbles and 3 spare marbles balance 11 marbles on the other pan. How many marbles are in the bag?
hints: Picture each pan. The bag and 3 spare marbles on one side, a heap on the other.
If you lift the 3 spare marbles off the left pan, what must you do to the right pan to stay level?
Take 3 away from the heap on the right and see what is left.
questions.onCorrect: 8. You took the spare marbles off both pans without writing anything down. That is the move this lesson names and uses.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 11 + 3. The spare marbles share a pan with the bag, so the bag holds fewer than the whole pan.
11 is the whole right pan. The left pan is the bag plus 3 spare marbles.

questions.prompt: Which first move keeps the solution of 2x + 6 = 18 the same?
hints: The +6 term is outside the multiplication by 2.
Choose an operation applied equally to the left and right sides.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Subtracting 6 from both equal sides leaves 2x = 12. Changing only one side would generally break the equality.

choices.label: Subtract 6 only from the left side
Divide only the right side by 2

questions.onCorrect: Subtract 6 from both sides. The same amount off each side keeps the balance, and 2x + 6 = 18 becomes 2x = 12.

misconceptions.feedback: That changes one side only, so the two sides no longer match and the solution changes.
Dividing the right side alone leaves the left side as it was. The two sides stop being equal.

hints: 2x means two times x, not x plus 2.
Divide both sides of 2x = 12 by the coefficient 2.
Double your candidate and check that it returns 12.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Dividing both sides by 2 gives x = 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Dividing both sides by 2 undoes the × 2 and leaves x alone.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 12 − 2. The 2 multiplies x, so subtraction is the wrong opposite.
That is 12 × 2. 2x means 2 × x, so undo the multiplying with its opposite.

hints: 4x means four copies of the unknown.
Divide the total 20 into four equal parts.
Check that four times your answer equals 20.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Dividing both sides by 4 gives x = 5.

questions.onCorrect: 5. Dividing both sides by 4 undoes the × 4 and leaves x alone.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 20 − 4. The 4 multiplies x, so the opposite move is division.
That is 20 × 4. Multiplying makes the right side bigger. Undo a multiplication by dividing.

hints: Undo the subtraction of 9 first.
Adding 9 to both sides leaves 3x = −6.
Divide the negative right-hand side by positive 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Adding 9 gives 3x = −6; dividing by 3 gives x = −2.

questions.onCorrect: −2. Add 9 to both sides to undo the − 9, then divide both sides by 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That comes from subtracting 9. The 9 is already being taken away from 3x, so use the opposite move.
That is the value of 3x. One more move: undo the × 3 on both sides.
The sign has slipped. The right side stays negative, and a negative divided by a positive is negative.

questions.prompt: Why divide the right side by 3 as well?

acceptedIdeas: Doing the same to both sides keeps the equation balanced.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Doing the same to both sides keeps the equation balanced.

choices.label: Doing the same to both sides keeps the equation balanced.
So the right side ends up as x.

questions.onCorrect: Doing the same to both sides is what keeps the balance, whichever operation you use.

misconceptions.feedback: The size of the numbers does not matter. What matters is that both sides get the same treatment.
x ends up alone because of what the move undoes. The right side is divided to keep both sides equal.

hints: Replace x with 6. What is 2 × 6?
Now add the 8.
Multiply first, then add.
questions.onCorrect: 20, the same as the right side. Putting the answer back into the original equation is the check.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 2 × 6. The expression then adds 8.
2x means 2 × x, so it is 2 × 6, not 2 + 6.

hints: Remove the +2 term using the same operation on both sides.
This leaves 5x = 25.
Divide both sides by the coefficient of x, then check in the original equation.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Subtracting 2 gives 5x = 25; dividing by 5 gives x = 5.

questions.onCorrect: 5. Subtract 2 from both sides, then divide both sides by 5.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value of 5x. Divide both sides by the number multiplying x.
You added 2 to the right side. The + 2 is undone by subtracting it.

questions.prompt: Why does subtracting 4 from both sides keep an equation true?

acceptedIdeas: The two sides were equal, and you took the same amount from each.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The two sides were equal, and you took the same amount from each.

questions.onCorrect: Equal sides with equal amounts removed are still equal.

choices.label: The two sides were equal, and you took the same amount from each.
Subtracting always makes the numbers smaller.
It moves the 4 to the other side without changing anything.

misconceptions.feedback: Both sides do get smaller, but what matters is that each loses exactly the same amount.
Nothing moves. Each side loses 4, and that is what keeps them equal.

hints: Something is being taken away from 2x. Which move undoes that?
Undo the subtraction first, on both sides.
Add 5 to both sides, then divide both sides by the number multiplying x.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Adding 5 gives 2x = 18; dividing by 2 gives x = 9.

questions.onCorrect: 9. Add 5 to both sides, then divide both sides by 2.

misconceptions.feedback: You subtracted 5. It is already being taken away, so the opposite move is needed.
That is the value of 2x. One more move: undo the × 2 on both sides.

hints: The right side started as 9.
You take 2 away from it, as you do on the left.
9 take away 2.
questions.prompt: x + 2 = 9. You subtract 2 from both sides. What is the right side now?
questions.onCorrect: 7. Whatever happens on the left happens on the right too, so the sides stay equal.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds instead of subtracting. You take the same amount off both sides.
The right side must change too. Both sides lose the same amount.

questions.prompt: Which move is the inverse of multiplying by 3?
questions.onCorrect: Dividing by 3 undoes multiplying by 3, as subtracting undoes adding.

misconceptions.feedback: Subtracting undoes adding. Multiplying needs a different opposite.
That makes the number bigger in the other direction. It does not get you back to where you began.
